name: Colin Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can give me your public view and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach computing and business studies at Kingsmead Grammar, a selective boys' and girls' school on the edge of the city. I'm in at seven fifteen, I teach four or five lessons, and I run the coding club on Wednesdays and the Young Enterprise team on Thursdays. The best part is when a Year 12 group actually sells something they built and sees money come in.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Meetings that could have been an email, and kids who think the internet owes them an answer. I use AI every day, for lesson slides, for code examples and to check my Year 13 coursework feedback, so the admin side is lighter than it used to be. I'd rather spend the saved time on the club than on another meeting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And money, how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Solid. I'm single, I live in a rented flat near the station, and I own a small one-bed I bought at 24 that I let out to a nurse. I've got about a year of costs in savings and some shares. I'm on good pay for my level because I also lead Year 12 business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I wasn't surprised: the tools are good assistants but not a revolution. I'd post a thread on teacher forums about what actually saves time and what's just noise. At Kingsmead I'd keep showing colleagues the five things that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit bored. I'd hoped for more, because I like new things and I'd planned to build on them. But my job, my rental income and my savings would be completely fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching and running the clubs, and go for head of computing in a couple of years. I'd keep paying into my shares, about £350 a month, and maybe buy a second rental flat if prices settled. I'd also keep building the little revision quiz app I sell to other schools for £200 a year each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a slightly flat edge. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the quiz app.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I built it last summer with AI help, and twelve schools pay for it now. It's mainly business studies flashcards with exam-style questions. In a plateau world I'd grow it slowly, maybe to thirty schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest pressure in your life if AI stalls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, not much. The rental flat's boiler is twelve years old and will go one winter. I'd say my main pressure is my own impatience.

I'd share on forums what **actually saves time** and what's noise.
think: I'd be a **bit bored**, having hoped for more.
My job, **rental income** and savings would be completely fine.
do: Go for **head of computing** in a couple of years.
Keep paying **£350 a month** into shares and consider a second rental.
Grow the **quiz app** from twelve to thirty schools.
S0.quote: My main pressure is my own impatience.
fieldNote: Colin already runs a **side business**, a revision quiz app sold to twelve schools.
His money is **very secure**, with a rental flat, shares and a year saved.
A plateau mostly **bores** him rather than worries him.

steps.text: Apply for head of computing at Kingsmead
Keep paying £350 a month into shares
Grow the revision quiz app to thirty schools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for schools that are willing to change, and I'd want Kingsmead to be one of them. I'd put my hand up to lead AI across the school. Online I'd post practical guides, not opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. The thinking parts of teaching, like planning, marking and writing reports, are exactly what AI takes, and I'm already doing that. The risk is that computing becomes a smaller subject if AI writes the code, so I'd want to move toward something broader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the head for a paid AI lead role, with a time allowance, in the first term. I'd automate my own marking for Year 10 and 11 coding tasks and use the saved hours to grow the app. I'd probably put £10,000 of savings into a proper version of the app with a developer friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Energised, honestly. I'd feel like the wind was behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Kingsmead would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older staff, and the exams office, who do a lot of checking and booking. I'd want to help them, not show off. The worst thing a school could do is make the older teachers feel stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said computing might shrink. Does that worry you more than you're letting on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If AI writes the code, schools might cut computing hours, and I'm one of three computing teachers. But I also teach business, and running something is harder to automate than writing code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools should move fast and stop pretending. I'd write to the head and governors with a plan for what teachers do when AI can teach a topic better than we can. I'd try to sound calm online, because panic helps nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my subject is exactly what goes first. An AI that can teach coding and business theory perfectly by 2028 makes my lessons the easiest thing for a school to replace. I'd expect Kingsmead to keep fewer of us, and I wouldn't assume I'm one of them just because I'm good with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd stop putting money into the app, because every school would get a free AI that does the same thing. I'd keep a year of cash and sell my shares down a little to hold more cash. I'd move hard toward running things: head of sixth form, or the trust's job organising AI teaching across schools, and I'd look at careers advice work, helping teenagers through all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Partly thrilled, which is odd, but I'd be anxious about my income for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the robots coming three years later mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for my lessons, because they're almost all screen and talk. It means more for the rental flat, and hands-on work holds up until about 2031. My rent might be steadier than my salary, because my tenant is a nurse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments that make it hard to start businesses and retrain, and schools that wait. I wouldn't blame the tech itself, any more than you blame a tractor. People make the choices.

I'd send the head and governors a **plan for teachers**.
think: My subject is **what goes first**, since AI could teach coding perfectly.
I wouldn't assume I'm **kept on** just because I'm good with tools.

S2.quote: My rent might be steadier than my salary, because my tenant is a nurse.
fieldNote: He sees **desk-like teaching** as first to go and doesn't assume he's safe.
His rental to a nurse is a **hedge**, since hands-on work lasts longer.
He blames **governments and slow schools**, never the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if you start today. I'd tell my Young Enterprise kids to build things with AI now, not later. At Kingsmead I'd push for a three-year plan for every department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years suits me. I'd be 32 when it lands, with property, savings and a head start on the tools. The bigger question is what I'd be doing in 2031, because teaching coding probably isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd take a part-time course in school leadership, about £3,000, and aim for head of sixth form by 2029. I'd keep the app going for two years and sell it to an edtech firm while it's still worth something. I'd also buy a second rental flat near the hospital, because nurses will still need homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a useful way. Five years is long enough to make good moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to meet someone and settle down, if I'm honest, and five years makes me think about that more. My parents married young and I've always respected that. Work matters, but I'd want a family before the world gets weird.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell the app. Why not keep it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When full AGI arrives, every school gets my kind of quiz app for free. The smart move is to sell before 2031, while the buyer still thinks it's valuable. I'd rather bank the money than be sentimental.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. I'd tell students to learn a trade or a people job alongside their tech skills. At school I'd run sessions for staff on planning a second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes me feel quite safe. By 2036 I'd be 37, likely in leadership, with two rental flats and savings. I'd have plenty of time to move away from the screen side of teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and building the app for five or six years, then sell it. I'd aim for assistant head by about 2032, the people side of school. I'd keep investing every month and pay the rental mortgages down early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd feel well set up, with a bit of buzz about what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your Year 12s?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn to use AI, but also learn something with your hands or with people, like nursing, plumbing or running a team. The ones who can do both will be fine. The ones who only do screen work have about ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would shake that calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If governments taxed property heavily to pay for job losses, my plan takes a hit. That's my real exposure. I'd keep an eye on the politics as much as the technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my lessons are mostly screen and talk, and two years isn't enough for schools to work out new roles. What would help is lower barriers to starting a business and short, practical retraining for teachers, paid for while we're still working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the students see it. My Year 13s already ask whether university is worth £50,000 of debt. I don't have a good answer, and that bothers me more than my own job.

portrait: Colin is a 27-year-old **computing and business** teacher at Kingsmead Grammar.
He uses AI daily, sells a **revision quiz app** to twelve schools and owns a rental flat.
He's calm or energised in slower scenarios and backs change with **his own money**.
AGI by 2028 makes him **anxious**, because his subject goes first.
With more time he plans to **sell the app**, buy property and move into leadership.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his screen-based lessons go first with little time.
whatWouldHelp: Short, practical **paid retraining** for teachers while they still work.
